entry.title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
entry.content:
Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine

Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex

Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machineStart a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then runatuin resume

Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me.

These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on exe.dev, a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on.

It’s a familiar problem!

I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of .bash_history. But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds.

Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things.

Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily.

Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work.

Atuin Threads

That is why we built Atuin Threads.

Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop.

Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this.

Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, run your own, or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too.

Run atuin resume, and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post!

It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever.

Right now, we support

Claude Code Codex Pi Omp OpenCode

with more agents coming soon.

MCP

With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context.

Our MCP is available as atuin mcp, and can be automatically installed with

atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode

There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples:

Work that never shipped

I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better.

These sessions contain the code that never made it into main, as well as my initial prompts and iteration. Subsequent agents can use this to figure out exactly what I want, without me having to write up a giant spec.

Object store outage

With all the security issues going on in the industry recently, we rolled our keys as a precaution. One of the new object store keys did not have the correct permissions for avatar uploads! We didn’t notice straight away 😬

My daily Sentry triage agent picked up on it, and traced the failure down to a command run earlier that day. I hadn’t gotten around to reading it yet, but prompting another agent with

seeing some tigris avatar issues?

led to the agent discovering the previous investigation, highlighting the cause, and developing the fix much faster than if it had done the whole thing from scratch.

Forking threads across machines

Before releasing Threads, I did some testing on a variety of machines and setups.

One machine did not perform well. The agent investigating proposed that this was because of poor IO performance, but that it needed something with a faster disk to confirm.

I forked the session onto my MacBook, and it continued from exactly where it left off. With the faster SSD, the investigation concluded that slow disk was only part of the story - we could speed up imports elsewhere, too.

Once the benchmarks were complete, the thread running on the original machine could pull the results from the Mac and build a fix. I didn’t have to copy-paste anything or co-ordinate across machines, and the data is now part of the record of my work.

Teams

While this is tremendously useful as a solo engineer, it gets even more interesting with a team.

So much of what we do never makes it into Git, issue trackers, or documentation. The context behind that work ends up scattered across individual agent sessions. What if the rest of the team could learn from it too? What if we could hand off an agent thread just like a Git branch?

We’re building opt-in session sharing for teams, and would love to hear from folks using agents day to day. If this sounds useful to you, please get in touch!

While agents have radically changed my daily workflow, shell history isn’t going anywhere, and is arguably more useful than ever. Threads is an extension of the same idea that started Atuin in the first place - the history of your work should be useful, accessible, and yours to keep.

Threads is out in Atuin 18.24+

Install or update Atuin with curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | sh Run atuin resume to get started Use the MCP with atuin mcp install

Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions or feedback!

entry.title: Pharo in the Browser with WebAssembly
entry.content:
Loading Pharo…

Drop to file in or opena Smalltalk .st file, a Pharo .zip, or an .image with its .changes and its .sources

Iceberg's https:// clones, fetches, pulls and pushes, and Metacello's github:// loads, go to this CORS proxy: each request goes to the proxy's URL followed by the host and the path of the repository, such as github.com/pharo-project/pharo.git. The proxy sees the code and any credentials that pass through it, so choose only one that you run or trust: the user name and token that a push asks for go only through My proxy, or straight to the host with None, never through the site's default. With None, the requests go to the repository itself, which works only for a server that lets this page in (CORS). This browser keeps your choice; a link cannot set it.

This page needs JavaScript and WebAssembly.

entry.title: The Computer Graphics Book of Knowledge
entry.content: <doc fingerprint="a19813594ba88fe0"> <main>The Computer Graphics Book Of Knowledge<quote><head rend="h1">History of Computer Graphics (CG)</head> Computer Graphics (CG) was first created as a visualization tool for scientists and engineers in government and corporate research centers such as Bell Labs and Boeing in the 1950s. Later the tools would be developed at Universities in the 60s and 70s at places such as Ohio State University, MIT, University of Utah, Cornell, North Carolina and the New York Institute of Technology. The early breakthroughs that took place in academic centers continued at research centers such as the famous Xerox PARC in the 1970¹s. These efforts broke first into broadcast video graphics and then major motion pictures in the late 70¹s and early 1980¹s. Computer graphic research continues today around the world, now joined by the research and development departments of entertainment and production companies. Companies such as George Lucas¹s Industrial Light and Magic are constantly redefining the cutting edge of computer graphic technology in order to present the world with a new synthetic digital reality. 1940s The very first ³computer assisted² graphics began in many different unrelated fields around the world. There is a very blurred line that is crossed somewhere between mechanical and analog computer assisted graphics, and the first directly digital computer generated graphics that would associate with today as being true ³CG². The very first radiosity image. While at MIT in the 1940s, Professors Parry Moon and Domina Eberle Spencer were using their field of applied mathematics to calculate highly accurate global lighting models which they called ³interflection reflection². The illumination algorithms were based on those by H. H. Higbie, published in his 1934 book, Lighting Calculations. Lacking any display or output mechanism, the image itself was created by painstakingly selecting Munsel paper samples that matched the output data of their mathematical model. The paper was cut out and ironed together by hand to create the image shown here in print for the first time in over 50 years. [IMAGE OF THE RADIOSITY PIC] (The original image is still hanging in the office of Dr. Domina Spencer at the University of Connecticut.) The images were first presented at the 1946 National Technical Conference of the Illuminating Engineering Society of North America, and published two years later (in color) in the book: Lighting Design by Moon, P., and D. E. Spencer. 1948. (Addison-Wesley. Cambridge, MA) The book was used for many years to teach lighting theory at MIT in the architecture curriculum there. Dr. Spencer went on to teach at Tufts, Brown, Rhode Island School of Design, and the University of Connecticut where she remains active today. 1950s John Whitney Sr. devises his own computer assisted mechanisms to create some of his graphic artwork and short films. One of his sons John Jr. works with and learns from his father from childhood through high school.see biography Pioneering artists Stan VanderBeck, Michael Noll and others at Bell Labs in New Jersey created computer assisted graphics using analog computer devices and plotter output. Later, in the mid 1960s, digital computers and film recorders would be used to produce some of the earliest CG animated films Bill Fetter experimented with early vector graphic CAD at Boeing (Seattle) in the late l950s using an IBM 7094 computer with punch card input and a Gerber plotter. 1950 Artist Ben Laposky uses analog computers to help him create oscilloscope artwork. 1951 Vectorscope-type graphics display on the Whirlwind computer at MIT. A device similar to a light pen allowed direct input to the screen. The General Motors Research Laboratory begins to study the role of computer aided graphical design applications. (This would later result in the development of the DAC-1) 1955 SAGE system at MITs Lincoln Lab uses the first true light pen as input device. (Bert Sutherland) 1956 Lawrence Livermore National Labs connects graphics display to IBM 704; use film recorder for color images Bertram Herzog at the University of Michigan Computing Center uses analog computers to generate CRT graphic studies of military vehicle behavior. 1957 1st image-processed photo at National Bureau of Standards. (By whom? Why?) The IBM 740-780 (paired with a separate IBM 704 computer system) generated a sequence of points on a CRT in order to represent lines or shapes. Time lapse film photography was used to capture the images as they were drawn on the screen. The Defence Departments Advanced Research Project Agency (ARPA) is founded. 1958 MIT¹s Lincoln Labs: Funded in part by the Air Force; Steven Coons, Ivan Sutherland, and Timothy Johnson begin working with the TX-2 computer system to manipulate drawn pictures. Ivan Sutherland later began refining the work into his famous Sketchpad system while a student at MIT. DEC later commercialized the TX-2 as the PDP-6. 1959 The first commercial film recorder the General Dynamics Stromberg Carlson 4020. (Produced in San Diego, CA.) 1959 DAC-1 (Design Augmented by Computers): First computer aided drawing system. Created by Don Hart and Ed Jacks at General Motors Research Laboratory and IBM. (Not unveiled until the Fall Joint Computer Conference in Detroit in 1964.) The system was originally based upon a IBM 7090 computer (later upgraded to a 7094 in 1963) augmented with extra disc space and a specially designed IBM 7969 ³image processing system². Input was with punch cards, but was also capable of scanning in drawings. The final data could be output to either 35mm film (by way of a CRT), a hard copy plotter, or used to drive computer controlled machining devices. Biography: John Whitney Sr. (1917-1995) A Los Angeles native, Whitney was a pioneer in many forms of experimental and abstract art before turning to computers to aid in his graphic creations. He attended Pomona College in California in the 1940's and was the first in a wave of artists to begin new techniques of computer assisted graphics. The integration of analog computer controlled camera and artwork were at first more a pioneering use of motion control than of computer graphics. In point of fact, the devices these early artists used were not even thought of as computers, being more akin to analog music synthesizers. From his experience working in the aircraft industry during World War II, Whitney realized that components of a computerized anti-aircraft controller could be used to drive his mechanisms. One of his sons (John Jr.), recalled buying the ³state-of-the-art² M7 anti-aircraft control computer at surplus. The still unopened crate was 12 feet long, 7 feet wide and seven feet tall. These synchronized mechanisms would ultimately be used to calculate abstract shapes, and change them over time to create beautifully abstract forms and animation. In the 1950¹s Whitney worked in Hollywood as an animation director at UPA, most notably contributing graphic elements for the Saul Bass designed opening credits to Hitchcock¹s ³Vertigo². Whitney then founded Motion Graphics Inc. in 1960 and produced animation for both television and film, devising the ³slit scan² technique for his early short film ³Lapis². This technique would later be made famous when used by Con Pederson as a portion of the famous ³StarGate² ending sequence of Stanley Kubrick¹s ³2001: A Space Odyssey². In 1966 with the help of a grant from IBM and a Fortran programmer named Jack Citron(sp?), Whitney made his first digital computer short film called "Permutations". His next works: Matrix 1 and Matrix 2 were done at Cal Tech, followed by Matrix 3 at Triple-I in 1971. It was at this time that he met Larry Cuba who would later be asked by Whitney to collaborate with him in 1975 on his last 16mm film project ³Arabesque², funded in part by an NEA grant. Both Whitney and Cuba would work briefly at Robert Abel¹s effects company before digital computer graphics were begun there. Beginning in the mid 1980's, a new collaborator Jerry Reed(sp?) translated Cuba¹s Fortran code into Pascal for use on new personal computer hardware that Whitney could use at home. Whitney continued to create abstract computer animation on his own with the aid of this new PC technology that freed him from the reliance of large company owned mainframe machines and the need for sponsored grants. His work would be displayed in galleries on the same PC hardware he created it on. His last commercially available collection of works, called ³Moondrum² was released on video in the late 1980¹s. Today his son Michael Whitney is serving as archiver for his fathers work, and recently organized a retrospective showing at UCLA. 1960's ³Computer assisted graphics² were being created more widely as a new and unique art-form by people such as Charles Csuri, Ken Knowlton and John Whitley Sr. Many pioneering artistic films and artworks were created at Bell Labs from about 1962 to 1967 by artists and programmers such as E.E.Zajac, Leon D. Harmon, Ken Knowlton, A.Michael Noll, Lilian Shwartz, M.R. Schroeder and Stan Vanderbeek. An IBM 7094 computer ran a Stromberg-Calson 4020 film recorder, programmed in FORTRAN to run Ken Knowltons Beflix animation system. Much of the nation-wide university computer science research conducted at the time was due in part to funding from the government¹s "Advanced Research Project Agency" (ARPA). ARPA at the time took a very hands-off approach to funding. This allowed researchers an un-pressured environment in which to concentrate on the work, without the heavy bureaucracy, paperwork and political constraints more common today. Much to the benefit of researches was Ivan Sutherland who headed ARPA for a time. With good funding, little oversight and many brilliant young minds inspiring each other, it was a unique and special time that produced the very foundation of today¹s computer graphic tool sets. Herb Freeman had a school of CG development going on at NYU including Alvy Ray Smith in his first professor's job out of Stanford in 1969. Freeman and his students had already solved the hidden-line problem, a very big deal at the time. [Quote] ³Also on the pixel side of things, Azriel Rosenfeld at the Univ of MD, and Ron Baecker was developing some of the very first computer animation. I saw his system GENESYS at an NYU demo in the early 1970s which means Ron probably did the development (in Canada, Toronto, I think) in the late 1960s.² -Alvy Ray Smith Nicholas Negroponte teaches Computer Aided Design (CAD) at M.I.T in the mid to late 60s, and develops the URBAN5 system. A light pen allows interaction directly on the CRT, in combination with keyboard instructions. Points and symbols are added in orthographic mode with a perspective option entered after the fact in order to view structures three-dimensionally. An ³intelligent² system study, URBAN5 was abandoned by 1968 in favor of other projects. ³The Society for Information Displays² is formed in the early 60s, publishing papers dealing mostly with military applications. At this same time, practical commercial and industrial use of computer graphics begins to take hold in many areas of design and manufacturing. Throughout the decade at Boeing, William Fetter and Robert Woodruff (Computing Technology Administrator) leads many important industrial applications of vector generated CG. Architectural and urban planning programs (typically written in FORTRAN on machines like the IBM 1130 or 1800) are used at the firm ³Skidmore, Owings & Merrill² in Chicago and in the University of Texas School of Architecture. A sample workstation would consist of a Rand tablet providing input, with output to pen plotters such as the Calcomp. In the late 60s, the Electronics Laboratory of General Electric (Syracuse, NY) produces a prototype visualization system for NASA and the Office of Naval Research. The system produced real-time color raster graphics on a monitor as a training aid to astronauts going to land on the moon. This same system was used by Prof. Peter Kamnitzer of the UCLA School of Architecture and Urban Planning to simulate urban development plans. Biography: Dr. Dave C. Evans (1924-1998) MORE One of a very few who could be called a true "founding father" of computer graphics, Dave Evans is perhaps best know for being the co-founder of "Evans & Sutherland Computer Corporation". Mr. Evans was at one time chairman of the computer science departments at both the University of California Berkeley and University of Utah, where he started the venerable doctoral program that would give birth to so much of the foundation of our industry. Evans first associated with Ivan Sutherland at both Berkeley and the Pentagon's "Advanced Research Project Agency" (ARPA). Mr. Evans made many contributions to a wide range of computer technologies, and a great many of his students went on to flourish in the brand new field of computer graphics, becoming true pioneers themselves. Students of Mr. Evans include Alan Kay(Co-founder of Xerox PARC), Jim Clark (founder of both Silicon Graphics and Co-founder of Netscape Communications), John Warnock(Co-founder of Adobe Systems) and Edwin Catmull(see biography in Programming chapter). Dave Evans passed away on Oct.3rd, 1998. 1960 William Fetter of Boeing coins the term "computer graphics" for his human factors cockpit drawings. With help from Walter Bernhardt, and others, Fetter input an aircraft drawing¹s coordinates into a database and plotted out a calculated perspective on a ³Illustromat 1100² plotter. John Whitney Sr. founds Motion Graphics, Inc. in LA. 1961/62 Spacewar: The first popular computer graphic game written by students Steve Russell, Slug Russell, Shag Graetz, and Alan Kotok of MIT to run on the DEC PDP-1. (DEC's PDP-1 cost $120,000 and MIT¹s was one of only 50 ever built) The large round CRT display featured graphics controlled by primitive handmade joysticks. The object being to maneuver away from a gravitational ³sun² force at the center, and avoid the other enemy ships, while trying to blast him with your own space torpedoes! The original source code (which ran on 4k of memory!) can still be found at www.media.mit.edu/groups/el/projects/spacewar/sources or ftp://ftp.digital.com/pub/DEC/sim/sources/sim_2.3d.tar.Z There's also a copy of the PDP-1 manual at www.dbit.com/~greeng3/pdp1/pdp1.html 1962 "Sketchpad: A Man-Machine Graphical Communication System" is presented by Ivan Sutherland as his Ph.D. thesis at the M.I.T. Lincoln Laboratory. The user could input simple lines and curves by drawing directly on the screen with a light pen. The computer, the TX-2, had a whopping 320 kilobytes of memory and a 9 inch monochromatic CRT. While Sketchpad was strictly 2D, a few years later Timothy Johnson expanded its capabilities into three dimensions as ³Sketchpad 3². The display CRT was divided up into the now familiar four views, top front side and perspective. ARPA J.C.R. Licklider is put in charge of the new Information Processing Techniques Office (IPTO) at the Defense Departments Advanced Research Project Agency (APRA). The initial $14 million dollar budget supported projects at MIT, Berkeley and Carnegie-Mellon. 1963 Biography: Ivan Sutherland Born in 1938, Hastings, Nebraska; Ivan Sutherland is truly an early ³founding father² of computer graphics. After completing his Ph.D. at M.I.T.(where he developed Sketchpad) in 1963, Ivan Sutherland joined the army and was assigned to the NSA as an electrical engineer. One year later, he was transferred to the Defense Department's Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA, later DARPA), and given responsibility for the newly-established Information Processing Techniques office. At age 26, Lt. Sutherland was given a secretary and $15 million a year, and was told to "go sponsor computer research." Which he gladly did for the following two years until joining the faculty at Harvard late in 1966. It was here with student Bob Sproull that they developed the Head Mounted Display (HUD), for remote viewing; the first ³Virtual Reality². In 1968 Ivan formed the Evans & Sutherland company with partner Dave Evans. Ivan was now a part time tenured professor at the University of Utah, where Evans was the founding head of the Computer Science Department. Dr. Sutherland had first met Evans during a visit to U.C. Berkeley as part of his ARPA work. Ivan's last research in computer graphics was a paper titled: "A Characterization of Ten Hidden-Surface Algorithms," by Sutherland, Sproull and Schumacker. The paper solved many of the largest problems of the day in this critical area of rendering and display technology. Later, as co-founder (with Carver Mead) and head of the Department of Computer Science at California Institute of Technology from 1976 - 1980, Dr. Sutherland developed and promoted courses involving integrated circuit design, the seed of knowledge that helped create the Silicon Valley industry. In the early 1980s at Carnegie Mellon University, Ivan did some research on a six legged walking robot, large enough to carry a driver. (And controlled by a joy stick acquired by brother Bert from his contacts in the Navy as a former fighter pilot!) In 1980, Ivan and Bob Sproull had started the consulting firm ³Sutherland, Sproull & Associates². Sun bought the company in 1990, which then became the nucleus of Sun Microsystems Laboratories. Today? Charles Csuri created an analogue computer and used it to make transformations of a drawing. He completed a series of drawings based upon the paintings of old masters such as Durer, Goya, Ingres, Klee, Mondrian and Picasso Ken Knowlton's programs BEFLIX and EXPLOR are used to create early computer films at Bell Telephone Labs. The 1st computer art competition, sponsored by Computers and Automation magazine. The Spring Joint Computer Conference has several people from MIT presenting papers on graphical display technology: Steven Coons, Ivan Sutherland, Tim Johnson, Bob Stotz, Doug Ross and Jorge Rodriquez. John Lansdown pioneered the use of computers as an aid to architectural planning, making perspective drawings on an Elliott 803 computer in 1963, modelling a building's lifts and services, plotting the annual fall of daylight across its site and authoring his own Computer Aided Design applications. Edgar Horwood developed a computer graphic mapping system used by the U.S. Housing and Urban Development. HUD publishes ³Using Computer Graphics in Community Renewal² Frieder Nake at The Computer Institute of the Stuttgart Polytechnic uses the Graphomat Zuse Z 64 Drawing machine to produce 4 color plotter drawings. 1964 [QUOTE] ³I did my first computer graphic at the Physical Sciences Lab at New Mexico State University. I was asked to generate an equiangular spiral antenna for one of the early Nimbus weather satellites. The old engineers asked me, a student, to do the tedious hand-drawing. I got a computer to draw the spiral quickly, amazing the old-timers.² Alvy Ray Smith Ivan Sutherland (a recent MIT gradute) takes over at the Information Processing Techniques Office (IPTO) at ARPA. It is suggested by his predisesor J.C.R. Licklider to take on a 'deputy', Bob Taylor. (The office¹s budget would reach $30 million by 1969, when it was changed to DARPA the Defense.) Sutherland transitions out of his office by early 1966 to go to Harvard, leaving Bob Taylor in charge. (Bob Taylor would later go on to play a key role in staffing the famous Xerox PARC.) 1965 Dr. David Evans founds the Computer Science Department at the University of Utah Ohio State University CG program started by Charles Csuri. 1st computer art exhibition, at Technische Hochschule in Stuttgart Bella Julesz and A.Michael Noll exhibit for the 1st U.S. computer art exhibition, at Howard Wise Gallery in New York (April, 1965) 196? First commercially available graphics computer: IBM 2250 (When was the DEC 338??) [FACTOID COSTS] A typical graphic display CRT cost about $40,000 US. Rand input tablets are about $10,000 US, and Calcomp plotters about $4000 US. 1966 "Odyssey": The first consumer computer graphics games product by Ralph Baer of Sanders Associates. Later marketed at Magnavox. Permutations: With a grant from IBM and a Fortran programmer named Jack Citron(sp?), John Whitney Sr. made the first digital computer short film. An IBM 2250 Graphic Display Console created dot patterns which were then recorded onto black and white 35mm film. The filmed images were then further enhanced with a specially designed optical printer to add secondary motion and color. As Associate Professor at Harvard, Ivan Sutherland and his students, Bob Sproull, Jim Clark and others, took earlier "Remote Reality" vision systems of the Bell Helicopter project, and turned it into what we now call Virtual Reality by replacing the camera with computer images. The first such computer environment was no more than a wire-frame room with the cardinal directions -- North, South, East, and West initialed on the walls. The viewer could "enter" the room by way of the West door, and turn to look out windows in the other three directions. Affectionately called ³The Sword of Damocles² because of its ceiling mounted gear, what they called the "Head- Mounted Display," later became known as Virtual Reality. The International Conference on Design and Planning: ³Computers in Design and Communication² is held at the University of Waterloo (Ontario). Organized by Professors Constant and Krampen of the Design Department, it was brought together to enlighten and inform designers of emerging computer technologies. 1967 [QUOTE] ³At the same time that geometry-based computer graphics (CG) was being invented so was sampling theory-based computer graphics, often called image processing (IP) or imaging. In the early days, two conferences - one for each half of the discipline - would be held side by side. One of the earliest journals was called Journal of Computer Graphics and Image Processing. Its editors were Herb Freeman and Azriel Rosenfeld (CG and IP, respectively). The earliest paper that I actually have in possession on IP side is ³Processing of Tiros Cloud Cover Pictures on a Digital Computer² by Albert Arking, 1967, but I'm sure the literature is much older. It's easy for the geometry based guys to leave all this stuff out and vice versa.² Alvy Ray Smith Allen Bernholtz and William Warntz of the Laboratory for Computer Graphics and Spacial Analysis at Harvard University use computer graphics to study layout and sound patters for hospital floorplans. Cornell University's School of Architecture is founded by Professor Donald Greenberg. Charles Csuri creates his famous ³Hummingbird² film. A ten minute long, vector interpolated 16mm film animation that is later purchased by the Museum of Modern Art as part of their permanent collection. 2D morphing techniques used were started by Les Mezei at the University of Toronto The MIT Center for Advanced Visual Studies is founded by Gyorgy Kepes The Computer Technique Group in Tokyo Japan is funded at the IBM Scientific Data Center. Engineers and designers create many beautiful and varied computer graphic art works, using image processing and geometric transformations. Members include Koji Fujino, Junichiro Kakizaki, Masao Komura, Fujio Niwa, Makoto Ohtake, Haruki Tsuchiya, and Kunio Yamanaka. Stephen Coons is Associate Professor of Mechanical Engineering at M.I.T., where he heads the computer aided design (CAD) group. He invents a method for patch continuity 1968 Robert Mallary, Professor at the Department of Art at the University of Massachusetts developed the TRAN2 computer program for calculating three-dimensional sculpture Cybernetic Serendipity: The Computer and the Arts exhibition at London Institute of Contemporary Arts (ICA) is organized by Jasia Reichardt. The first major public computer art show, Cybernetic Serendipity is also a book published at the same name. The UK's Computer Arts Society (CAS) is founded by John Lansdown at the Royal College of Art. The EVENT ONE computer art exhibition is held at the Royal College of Art. Chaired and organized by John Lansdown. CalComp (California Computer Products) holds a competition for the best ³Computer Plotter Art², with scholarship and cash prizes. The first computer animation in the UK was the FLEXIPEDE made by Tony Pritchett. Made at the Open University. Several computer art publications are available in Europe including Bit International out of Zagreb, and Page by the London Art Society, a monthly magazine which actually lasted until the mid 80s. Ivan Sutherland joins the Computer Science Department at University of Utah The very first computer graphics company was formed by two of the leading researchers of the day, Drs. David C. Evans and Ivan E. Sutherland. Aptly named Evans & Sutherland, it provided a vector system comprised of custom designed hardware and software previously available only to one of a kind, multi million dollar military sites. Dicomed is founded as a manufacturer of hardware and software products to apply computer graphic technology to the field of medical radiology. Their systems operate by scanning x-ray films, converting the information into digital data, enhancing it and redisplaying the processed image. (See their web site at www.dicomed.com ). Still in business 30 years later, providing professional high resolution digital image capturing technologies. entry.title: A false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
entry.content:
How a false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter

AI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits. Some tasteful imperfections kept to heighten Wabi-Sabi effect.

Everyoneâs heard of how awesome Jane Street is. Fewer people have heard about the times something stupid nearly put it out of business and it was saved by grit and dumb luck. I was on the systems team for some of those. Jane Street didnât do titles, and we on the systems team werenât above getting our hands dirty. You could think of us as the firmâs blue-collar OCaml programmers: when something broke, we were the ones running through the corridors to fix it. Call this story a Star Trek: Lower Decks view of Jane Street.

For the longest time Jane Street insisted on having its machine room close to its trading floor. When it was 10 people it was cute. When it was 150 people it was starting to feelâ¦ odd. Part of the reason for this was intellectual property concern: they didnât want to risk having their servers stolen by spies who would learn their precious trading strategies. Another reason was technology risk: they wanted to make sure out-of-control automated trading systems could always be shut down by running across the hall and pulling power cables.

Yes, tools existed to mitigate both of these fears. But Jane Street moved irritatingly slowly on this stuff, and they still wanted the last-resort option of yanking power cords. Their risk culture didnât exclusively come from reading heady thinkpieces. A lot of it was instilled by a partner whoâd served on a nuclear submarine, and it showed, mostly in a good way! On a sub, you donât trust the automation unless thereâs a big red-painted, mechanically connected lever you can pull to turn it off.

As the company grew this humble machine room was built out into a respectably sizable datacenter, complete with an online UPS, Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units, refrigerator-sized network switches, a subterranean diesel backup generator and about 10 rows of server cabinets, 10 cabinets deep. Oh, and it was all crammed into the middle of a skyscraper called 1 New York Plaza, which was otherwise just a normal office building.

When I first landed my job at Jane Street I was commuting to the southern tip of Manhattan all of the way from Queens, an hour or more each way. Iâd gone to a magnet high school in the city, so Iâd been doing commutes like that since I was a teenager, and I was tired of it.

Now that I was making big Wall Street money I decided Iâd get an apartment. A real estate agent kept trying to show me what they called âpanty droppersâ, but I was only interested in one thing: proximity to the office. I ended up in a 200 square foot studio that was a 9 minute commute on foot from my apartment door to my desk on the trading floor. I would weirdly boast about it to the rest of the systems team, but it also meant everyone at the office knew I was a stoneâs throw away in case there was an emergency.

And that day came soon enough. One evening after work, just as I was about to climb into the elevator at my apartment building, my phone rang. It was our Hong Kong office, and when Hong Kong had a New York problem, mine was (now) the number they called. The smoke alarm in our NYC datacenter had gone off.

We had contractors working on a prep room next to the datacenter. While cutting into stuff, some dust was kicked up and it set off the smoke alarm. This is bad, but not for the reason you might think. Office buildings have sprinklers in them for fire suppression. You may have seen it go off in movies where someone just holds a lit cigarette up to the sprinkler on the ceiling and it floods the entire room. In reality theyâre not quite that dumb, but itâs close.

Firstly, the sprinklers over a machine room like ours usually arenât kept full of water all of the time. This saves you from having to deal with any leaks that might develop overhead over the years. Secondly, the sprinkler heads donât have smoke sensors. Instead, a different system detects the smoke, and thatâs when the pipes fill with pressurized water, but they donât spray yet. What triggers the spray is heat: each sprinkler head has its own heat-sensitive plug, which opens once the air around it becomes hot enough. The logic is that the smoke alarm must be real, whatever fire triggered it hasnât been brought under control since itâs gotten very hot, and the sprinklers should douse it with water.

Of course, the ceiling of our datacenter was full of sprinklers set up exactly this way. Weâre still fine because even though contractors might have set the smoke detector off by kicking up dust, thereâs no actual fire producing heat, so the sprinklers wouldnât spray, right? Well, no. One final piece of this contraption is that if the smoke alarm detects smoke, it would be absolutely terrible to keep circulating air through the room since that would help feed any fires, so the smoke alarm is wired to shut down the CRAC units(!)

Can you see the problem now? Rooms full of computer racks have high cooling demands. If you shut down the cooling, the temperature starts climbing. If you have a bunch of sprinklers that have just become pressurized because of a smoke alarm, you now have a serious, potentially business-ending problem on your hands.

And so my mission was made clear: as fast as I possibly could, get back to Jane Street, get into the machine room, and pull the power cord on every device in that room before the temperature climbed past 150 F and the sprinklers destroyed everything.

I ran down the (ironically named) Water Street in the Financial District faster than probably anyone has ever run down it, mashed the elevator button in the lobby of 1 NYP, waited very impatiently for the elevator to climb the 33 floors, slammed my keycard against the reader, booked through the main office door, took a hard right turn to the machine room door, slammed my keycard against that, stepped into what felt like a sauna and went row by row, cabinet by cabinet, yanking power cables out with both hands.

Then I watched the temperature monitor. 141 F. 142. 143. 143.5. 143.6. Finally it stopped. A quiet Iâd never heard before set in on the machine room.

The machine room had been kept across the hall so that someone could always run in and pull the power cords. I doubt anyone had pictured doing it to save the servers from the goddamn sprinklers.

Since the major NYC markets were closed for the day, the downtime from this fiasco was minimal, and we were up and running the next morning.

There were a couple of meetings after that. You might picture Gordon Gekko coldly deciding whose career was over, but meetings at Jane Street were never like that. They were matter-of-fact, level-headed and honestly kind of fun, closer to engineering students in a college dorm arguing over what went wrong. The outcome of all that level-headed discussion: the sprinklers would stay, we would tighten up procedures and surveillance, and we would continue hosting servers in our office building right next to our trading floor. That is, until Hurricane Sandy smacked us upside the head, but thatâs a story for another day.

As for me, when the next morning came around I knew what had to be done. Our Hong Kong team had only caught the problem by luck: someone happened to see on a display that server after server was popping up a climbing temperature condition. No one server was configured to alert just because it was a little hot, since that happens from time to time. But an across the board increase in temperature on many servers means thereâs a generalized cooling failure.

What we needed was a system monitor built for this exact purpose, one we could trust to be ultimately, unfailingly reliable at the task of asking each Linux server for its temperature and computing a simple mean. Bash wouldnât cut it for this. Nor would Perl. No, a job of this magnitude called for the most reliable and type-safe programming language imaginable. So I fired up emacs and wrote it in good old OCaml: every minute, ask every server in each location directly for the temperature from its onboard sensors, take the average, and if itâs elevated, blast an alert out to everyone on the systems team to check for datacenter overheat.

Yes, we could have also alerted if the CRAC units shut down or if a dedicated temperature sensor in the room was high, but the telemetry for this stuff was nowhere near as reliable, and unknown unknowns can still ruin you, so the most durable thing sometimes really is to ask your fleet of Linux boxes for their temperature and freak out if the average is just a little too high.

Our team didnât interact much with the partner with the nuclear sub experience, but Iâd like to think he would have approved.

Got a better tale of woe? Let me know at X, Bluesky, Hacker News or Lobsters.

entry.title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
entry.content:
Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG

Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query.

As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution â a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs â rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs â is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently.

In Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions, a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) â once, offline, for a fixed database of keys â that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs.

The Basics of Maximum Inner Product Search

A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into k clusters â k is typically much smaller than the total number of keys n â keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these k centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has n keys and k evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of n/k â a factor-of- k speedup when compared to the n comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in Figure 1 below.

MIPS as a Support Function

What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the support function of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, input convex neural networks (ICNNs). Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself.

The broad idea behind this work is to learn a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input.

Two Ways to Learn Maximum Inner Product Search

If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best:

The SupportNet neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality.

KeyNet models learn to directly output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Eulerâs theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced.

Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter.

Learned Routing with SupportNet

As shown in Figure 1, the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each clusterâs centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these k scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match.

If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in Figure 2, in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings.

Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these k support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output k scores at once. We can then use the largest of these k scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: âHow good is the best key inside this cluster for this query?â SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values.

We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on Natural Questions partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup.

Figure 4 below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top-s clusters matched with the query, where s grows as powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, â¦, 128). Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters.

The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9Ã faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids.

The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90â93% of the time â up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) â versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline.

Plugging Into Existing Indices

SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a âquery rewriterâ in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in Figure 5: sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association.

We evaluated KeyNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L â 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) and in Figure 6 below, we show recallâcost tradeoffs for these different sizes. On the first tab, the search budget is wall-clock latency: reaching 99% recall takes up to ~8Ã less time with the largest model (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms for the raw query). As before, the second tab focuses exclusively on the boost in âqualityâ provided by replacing the original query with its KeyNet transformation. The x-axis is the fraction of the database the index actually scans: scanning just 0.001% of the database, KeyNet-mapped queries retrieve the true key 89â97% of the time â up to 96.7% for the largest model (L) â versus 86% for the raw query, and reaching 99% recall takes up to ~11Ã fewer keys (0.009% vs 0.10% raw). Better recall for the same cost, or the same recall for a fraction of it.

We show examples obtained from the same Natural Questions dataset discussed previously, served through a FAISS IVF index. It is one of several datasets we studied, and the trend is consistent across them. Querying the index with KeyNetâs predicted key consistently beats querying with the raw question, across the full search-budget sweep.

Namely, Figure 7 below shows five Natural Questions examples: top-3 hits for the raw query versus the KeyNet-mapped query.

Which Network Should You Use?

The choice between the two ends up being a practical one. Use KeyNet when inference speed is the bottleneck and you just need to approximate the best key. Use SupportNet when you also want a calibrated score (for re-ranking, thresholding, or downstream use), or when compute is tight at small model sizes â a regime where SupportNet stays competitive. Both train similarly, integrate with existing approximate-search infrastructure, and are reasonably robust to mild distribution shift in the query patterns. Ultimately, a very large-scale MIPS system for which the set of keys is huge may require both: train a SupportNet router over all clusters, and then one KeyNet per cluster to help its regular indices zero in on the best key faster.

A New Direction for Learned Retrieval

Amortized MIPS reflects a shift in how retrieval can be approached when query distributions are known in advance â a common condition in production ML systems. By encoding MIPS solutions directly into network weights, the approach trades a one-time training (so-called amortization) cost for fast, lightweight inference and opens a practical path toward learned retrieval systems explicitly tailored to the queries they serve.

entry.title: AWS Finally Built Its Own AWS Emulator
entry.content:
AWS Emulator is a local emulator of the AWS APIs. You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS.

The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead.

AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See Security in AWS Emulator.

Documentation: AWS Emulator User Guide

Install the aws-emulator skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See Getting started with an AI coding agent.

aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1 Linux: install the RPM or Debian package and run aws-emulator. See Getting started on Linux. Windows / macOS: run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See Getting started with Docker.

Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator.

Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See Getting started with embedded mode, and Building from source below for its build cost.

To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the releases page. To check whether your own project is expected to work, see Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator.

Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's issues/ directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under issues/things-that-do-not-work/, and ones that have since been fixed move to issues/things-that-now-work/.

You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see Quick start). Building from source is supported on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64); on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above.

A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via rustup). A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code. At least 100 GB of free disk for target/. The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added. A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster. cargo build -p aws-emulator-router cargo run -p aws-emulator-router

The emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 (self-signed certificate).

Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first cargo test builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and target/ on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across projects, cache target/ (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change.

. ├── Cargo.toml # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates ├── services/ │ └── service-<name>/ # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE │ ├── smithy-model/ # <name>.json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol │ ├── build.rs # generates the service declaration from the model │ ├── src/ │ │ ├── service.rs # request routing and refusal overrides │ │ ├── state.rs # this service's in-memory state │ │ └── ops/ # one file per operation │ └── tests/ ├── core/ │ ├── router/ # the emulator binary: mounts every service on one endpoint │ └── embedded/ # the in-process (embedded mode) facade ├── vendor/ # framework crates — do not edit (replaced on update) └── issues/ # tracked fidelity issues

AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default. AWS Emulator collects telemetry data with strict data minimization in mind, preventing identification or attribution to specific users, accounts, or organizations. Its records never include what’s in your requests or responses, your code, your credentials, or personal data. We don’t share telemetry with third parties.

For details on what is collected and how the data is handled, see Telemetry in AWS Emulator. To turn telemetry off, use one of the following options.

Start the emulator with the --telemetry option (short form -t) set to off. This setting applies only to that emulator process.

aws-emulator --telemetry off

In a container, add --telemetry off after the image name in the docker run command.

Set EMULATOR_TELEMETRY to off before you start the emulator. This setting applies to every emulator that you start from that shell.

EMULATOR_TELEMETRY accepts on, true, or 1 to turn telemetry on, and off, false, or 0 to turn it off. Values aren’t case sensitive. Any other value turns telemetry off, and the startup notice shows a warning.

export EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off aws-emulator

To turn telemetry off for every run on a machine, add these lines to the emulator settings file, config.toml. The file is ~/.aws/emulator/config.toml on Linux and macOS, and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\emulator\config.toml on Windows. To use a different file, set the EMULATOR_CONFIG environment variable to its path.

[telemetry] enabled = false

In embedded mode, turn off telemetry in the options that you pass when you create the emulator.

use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions, Telemetry}; fn main() { let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default().telemetry(Telemetry::Off)); let _http_client = emulator.http_client(); }

You might build a tool that includes the emulator, such as a test framework that other people run. If you do, tell your users about telemetry and give them a way to turn it off. You can also ship your tool with telemetry off.

Report bugs and fidelity gaps in GitHub Issues. The most useful report names the service, the operation, your SDK and version, the request you sent, and how the response differed from real AWS. This repository does not take PRs.
